entries.title: Parametric UMAP embeddings for representation and semi-supervised learning
entries.name: Parametric UMAP
aliases: Parametric Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
entries.definition: A parametric dimensionality-reduction algorithm that trains a neural mapping from input points to embedding coordinates using sampled attractive and repulsive losses derived from a UMAP neighborhood graph.
entries.mechanism: Construct locally scaled UMAP graph affinities, then optimize neural-network weights so the network outputs serve as embedding coordinates. Positive graph edges and sampled negative pairs supply a minibatch binary cross-entropy-style training loss; the learned mapping can embed new inputs by a forward pass. Reconstruction, classification or global-distance regularizers are optional extensions rather than necessary parts of the base algorithm.
entries.locator: Sections 2.1–2.4, PDF pp. 4–10; Section 4 and Figure 2, pp. 11–14; discussion, pp. 36–37
entries.identity_notes: The core distinction from AIMech:UMAP is optimization of a shared neural input-to-coordinate mapping, rather than one free coordinate vector per training point. A parametric t-SNE objective and a generic autoencoder are different constructions; the UMAP/autoencoder and supervised hybrids are optional variants.
limitations: The graph metric, neighborhood structure, network capacity, optimization and sampling affect the learned representation; a reusable mapping does not ensure reliable extrapolation to new distributions.

Minibatch negative sampling changes the effective loss relative to the nominal all-pairs fuzzy cross-entropy. The analyzed parametric loss has batch-size and degree-product factors, distinct from the nonparametric symmetrized loss.
A classifier regularized by graph structure requires a graph relevant to its labels; the paper does not establish universal semi-supervised improvement.
The specified paper and sampling analysis were inspected; current software, all supplementary results and universal topology preservation were not certified.

additional_evidence.title: On UMAP’s True Loss Function
additional_evidence.locator: Section 5, footnote 3 and Theorem 5.1, equation (13), PDF pp. 6–7
additional_evidence.claim: The sampling analysis distinguishes Parametric UMAP’s within-batch negative samples and gives a batch-size-dependent effective objective with degree-product repulsive weights. This differs from its nonparametric symmetrized objective and from nominal all-pairs cross-entropy; the result concerns the analyzed procedure, not every implementation.

entries.title: TriMap: Large-scale Dimensionality Reduction Using Triplets
entries.version: arXiv:1910.00204v2, revised 2022-03-26; updated method notes coexist with older-code experiments
entries.name: TriMap
entries.definition: A nonlinear dimensionality-reduction algorithm that selects weighted triplet comparisons from high-dimensional data and optimizes embedding coordinates to favor the corresponding ordering of pairwise similarities.
entries.mechanism: Sample neighbor-versus-farther triplets and additional randomly selected triplets ordered by input proximity. Weight triplets using input-distance differences and the version-specific smoothing rule. Minimize the sum of weighted s(i,k)/(s(i,j)+s(i,k)) losses with s(i,j)=1/(1+||y_i−y_j||²), commonly starting from scaled PCA coordinates and using momentum-based full-batch optimization. The inspected revision describes shifted tempered-log weights and updated triplet counts separately from older experimental settings.
entries.locator: Section 3, PDF pp. 4–5; version-update notice on p. 1; global-score definition, Section 2, pp. 3–4
entries.identity_notes: TriMap denotes the sampled triplet embedding algorithm, not a three-valued segmentation trimap, generic ordinal embedding, its PCA-based global score, or PaCMAP’s pair losses. Version updates to sampling and weights are retained as method variations, not silently mixed with the older experiments.
limitations: Triplet sampling, weighting, initialization and input metric influence the layout; minimizing the sampled objective does not guarantee satisfaction of every possible triplet or recovery of a unique manifold.

The v2 PDF says its displayed experiments use older code. It updates counts from 10×5+5 to 12×4+3 and replaces the earlier weight transformation; these are not results for a single identical software version.
Wang et al.’s initialization critique studies the older 55-triplet construction and should not be treated as a direct benchmark of every later revision.

The separately proposed global score is based on linear reconstruction relative to PCA; it is not a universal geometric-fidelity certificate, and its displayed normalization requires nonzero PCA residual error.

additional_evidence.title: Understanding How Dimension Reduction Tools Work: An Empirical Approach to Deciphering t-SNE, UMAP, TriMap, and PaCMAP for Data Visualization
additional_evidence.locator: Sections 3.3, 5.1 and 6.1–6.2, PDF pp. 10–11, 28–30 and 33–36; Figure 11, p. 29
additional_evidence.claim: Wang et al. challenge attributing global layout solely to the triplet loss: their analysis emphasizes initialization and the limited range of attractive and repulsive forces. Their inspected TriMap definition uses 55 triplets per point and the older exponential/log weight rule, so this qualification is version-scoped rather than a claim about all later code.

entries.name: PHATE
aliases: Potential of Heat Diffusion for Affinity-based Transition Embedding
entries.definition: A dimensionality-reduction algorithm that computes diffusion transition probabilities, measures Euclidean distances between their negative-log rows, and uses metric multidimensional scaling to embed those potential distances.
entries.mechanism: Build symmetric local affinities with an adaptive bandwidth and an alpha-decaying kernel, row-normalize them to a Markov operator P, and take a selected diffusion power P^t. For positive transition probabilities, form potential vectors −log(P^t_i) and their Euclidean pairwise distances. Initialize with classical MDS and optimize metric-MDS stress in the requested output dimension. The paper proposes an entropy-knee heuristic for choosing diffusion time and a separate landmark approximation for scaling.
entries.locator: Results overview, printed pp. 1482–1483 / PDF pp. 1–2; Methods, local affinities through MDS, equations (1)–(9), PDF pp. 12–14
entries.identity_notes: PHATE uses potential distances between transformed diffusion distributions followed by stress fitting; AIMech:DiffusionMaps uses time-scaled Markov eigenvectors. PHATE is not generic MDS, a generative diffusion model, a branch-detection procedure or the DEMaP evaluation criterion. The core algorithm is distinct from its landmark approximation and multislice extensions.
limitations: Neighborhood affinities, bandwidth, decay exponent and diffusion time determine the geometry; excessive diffusion can remove signal as well as noise.
Negative logarithms require positive entries. Disconnected or numerically thresholded transitions need explicit zero-handling; the paper’s formula alone does not specify a universal remedy.
A two- or three-dimensional stress fit can distort potential distances and does not guarantee global optimization, preservation of every manifold property or biological trajectories.

The entropy discussion assumes a nonnegative spectrum for its probability normalization. This record does not certify that assumption for every adaptive kernel or treat the knee heuristic as an optimal-time theorem.
The inspected PDF is marked corrected; the correction notice and access limitations are tracked in the discovery report.

entries.title: Visualizing Large-scale and High-dimensional Data
entries.version: WWW 2016 proceedings, pp. 287–297; Microsoft Research-hosted published PDF
entries.name: LargeVis
entries.definition: A dimensionality-reduction and graph-visualization algorithm that constructs an approximate weighted nearest-neighbor graph and learns low-dimensional coordinates with sampled attractive-edge and repulsive-pair likelihood terms.
entries.mechanism: Initialize approximate neighbors with random projection trees and refine candidate neighbors through neighbors-of-neighbors exploration. Assign locally normalized Gaussian weights with a perplexity-controlled bandwidth and symmetrize them. Model edge likelihood using a decreasing function of embedded distance, sample positive edges in proportion to their weights, draw negative endpoints with degree-to-the-three-quarters weighting, and optimize the sampled log objective using asynchronous stochastic gradients.
entries.locator: Sections 3.1–3.2, Algorithm 1 and equations (1)–(6), PDF pp. 3–5; Section 4.2 for the graph/visualization distinction
entries.identity_notes: LargeVis combines a specific approximate-neighbor construction with a probabilistic layout objective. It is distinct from t-SNE’s normalized KL objective, UMAP’s locally scaled graph weights, LINE graph representations, and generic nearest-neighbor search.
limitations: Graph construction is approximate; the reported near-perfect neighbor recovery on selected datasets is not a guarantee for arbitrary input.
The sampled objective in equation (6) replaces the all-negative-pairs expression in equation (5); it is not asserted to be an unbiased evaluation of every original negative term.

The linear layout-cost statement assumes fixed embedding dimension and negative-sample count with a number of updates proportional to points; it does not establish linear cost for all graph construction or convergence.
Perplexity, graph quality, negative distribution, optimizer and chosen low-dimensional probability function affect results. No universal geometric fidelity or benchmark superiority is asserted.

entries.title: Understanding How Dimension Reduction Tools Work: An Empirical Approach to Deciphering t-SNE, UMAP, TriMap, and PaCMAP for Data Visualization
entries.name: PaCMAP
entries.definition: A nonlinear dimensionality-reduction algorithm that embeds neighbor, mid-near and farther point pairs using separate attractive and repulsive losses whose relative weights change through three optimization phases.
entries.mechanism: Choose neighbors from a Euclidean-neighbor candidate pool using locally scaled distances, choose mid-near partners as the second closest among six sampled observations, and sample non-neighbors for farther pairs. With d̃=||y_a−y_b||²+1, use d̃/(10+d̃) for neighbors, d̃/(10000+d̃) for mid-near pairs and 1/(1+d̃) for farther pairs. Optimize with Adam, ordinarily from PCA initialization, first emphasizing mid-near attraction, then reducing it and finally setting its weight to zero while refining local structure.
entries.locator: Sections 3.4 and 7, PDF pp. 11–12 and 36–39; Algorithm 1, p. 37; initialization qualifications, Section 6.2, pp. 35–36
entries.identity_notes: PaCMAP uses three classes of pair losses and a changing phase schedule, rather than TriMap’s coupled triplet loss or UMAP’s fuzzy graph construction. The graph-sampling rules and phase weights are defining components, not a proof of universal local/global preservation.
limitations: Random sampling and the initial coordinates affect the result. The authors explicitly state that robustness to initialization is incomplete and that initialization scale matters.
A mid-near partner is selected by a six-point sample rule, not an exact global distance quantile; the method does not guarantee that every such partner is outside the nearest-neighbor set.
Locally scaled distances select neighbor pairs, while optimization uses embedded distances and pair-class weights; the original distances are not fitted as an all-pairs metric.
The three-phase procedure seeks a useful nonconvex layout. No global optimum, exact topology preservation, density preservation or universal performance advantage is asserted.

source_caveats.observation: The original nominal objective and negative-sampling explanation are qualified by Damrich and Hamprecht Theorem 5.1, not their nonparametric equation (12). The parametric analysis uses within-batch negatives and degree-product factors. The cached primary analysis was re-read on PDF pp. 6–7 and p. 7 was rendered and inspected.

v2 updates weight smoothing and defaults while explicitly retaining older-code experiments. Wang et al. describe the older 55-triplet and exponential/log weighting construction; their critique is not relabeled as an experiment on every current release.

The author-hosted PDF is marked corrected and equation (4) displays P rather than the erroneous tbfP. The publisher correction body returned by indexed search names an omitted affiliation and matrix formatting changes. Direct publisher access provided only preview metadata; the correction content is recorded as indexed publisher text, not a separately downloaded correction PDF.

Positive entries are required by the displayed log transform. The spectral-entropy derivation explicitly assumes nonnegative eigenvalues, which is not certified here for every adaptive kernel; no universal kernel PSD or optimal-time theorem is asserted. Metric-MDS stress may remain nonzero, as the source itself notes.

Equation (5) writes a product and a proportional log expression; these are optimization-related, not a literal algebraic proportionality. Equation (6) redefines a negative-sampled objective. Linear layout cost presumes fixed sample/dimension factors and proportional update count; approximate graph-construction cost remains distinct.

The locally scaled distance chooses neighbors from a Euclidean candidate pool; it is not the low-dimensional optimization distance. Mid-near sampling is second closest of six, not an exact quantile or guaranteed non-neighbor. Algorithm 1 uses three changing pair-class weights and Adam.

The densvis author page and original-repository metadata identify densMAP and den-SNE, but Nature full article access failed, PMC repeatedly presented reCAPTCHA, the author lab page timed out, and bioRxiv PDF returned HTTP 403. No access-control bypass was attempted. Both concepts remain pending accessible full methods or versioned implementation inspection, not declared absent or exhausted.

Parametric UMAP extraction emitted color-space warnings for embedded figures; relevant method equations were rendered and inspected. PHATE final pages 19–21 had little extractable text and were not used for method claims. No claim of all-page or complete-proof inspection is made.
